issues.legal_issue: An increase in rent and a change in its payment frequency do not, without clear evidence of an intention to end the existing lease, create a new tenancy that extinguishes a tenant’s accrued protection rights.
material_facts: The tenant had occupied the vacant site under an oral lease made before the tenant-protection law was extended to the area, and had erected buildings on it.
The landlord sought fixation of rent, and the parties jointly agreed to an increased rent payable monthly; they did not execute a new lease or otherwise alter the tenancy terms.
The landlord later argued that the rent agreement created a new tenancy, while the tenant relied on the original tenancy to claim protection in the ejectment proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The original tenancy continued; the increase in rent and change in payment frequency did not create a new tenancy or deprive the tenant of protection rights.
issues.legal_principle: A mere increase or reduction of rent does not necessarily imply surrender of an existing lease and grant of a new tenancy; consequential changes to the timing or manner of rent payment do not establish a new tenancy absent the parties’ intention to create one. Under Section 12 of the Madras City Tenants’ Protection Act, a contract cannot take away or limit the Act’s rights, so a claim that a protected tenancy was surrendered and replaced requires clear and compelling evidence. The Court relied on Gopulal v. Dwarkadheeshji and the principles stated in Halsbury’s Laws of England and Hill and Redman’s Laws of Landlord and Tenant. It distinguished Ranganathan v. Ethirajulu, Ganesa Mudaliar v. Chellammal, M. Devasakayam v. Thiruveedi Amman Koil Devasthanam, and Natesa v. Arumugha, which involved materially different circumstances or substantial changes to tenancy terms.

rule.if: tenant_protection_claim_in_ejectment_proceeding and pre_existing_tenancy_with_protection_rights and only_rent_or_payment_terms_changed and not clear_evidence_of_intended_new_tenancy

predicates.tenant_protection_claim_in_ejectment_pro: A tenant claimed statutory protection against a landlord’s effort to recover possession.
predicates.pre_existing_tenancy_with_protection_rig: The tenant’s possession and claimed protection rights arose from a tenancy that existed before the relevant protection applied.
predicates.only_rent_or_payment_terms_changed: The parties changed the rent or its payment schedule without making other substantial changes to the tenancy.
predicates.clear_evidence_of_intended_new_tenancy: The parties clearly demonstrated an intention to end the old tenancy and create a new one.

issues.definition: When a tenant claims protection in an ejectment proceeding, the original tenancy continues for protection if it predated the protection rights, the parties changed only rent or payment terms, and they did not clearly intend a new tenancy.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s claim to purchase the leased site may cover land used for non-residential buildings when protection is extended to those buildings while the claim remains pending.
material_facts: When the tenant filed the purchase application, protection in the area covered residential buildings but not the tenant’s non-residential building.
The tenant’s claim to protection for the non-residential portion remained in issue during the proceedings.
Before the proceedings concluded, the Government extended protection to tenants with non-residential buildings in the area.
issues.conclusion: The tenant was entitled to seek purchase of the entire leased site, including the portion used for the non-residential building.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3 and 9 of the Madras City Tenants’ Protection Act provide, respectively, for compensation for buildings on leased land and for a qualifying tenant to seek a court-ordered sale of the land needed for their convenient enjoyment. Because protection was extended to non-residential buildings while the proceedings remained pending and the tenant had kept the issue alive, the Court gave the tenant the full benefit of the extended protection.

predicates.tenant_purchase_claim_in_pending_proceed: A tenant’s request to purchase leased land under a tenant-protection scheme remained unresolved in pending proceedings.
predicates.protection_extended_to_nonresidential_bu: The protection scheme was extended to non-residential buildings before the pending claim was resolved.
predicates.tenant_claimed_protection_for_residentia: The tenant sought protection for land associated with both residential and non-residential buildings.

issues.definition: A tenant with a pending purchase claim covering residential and non-residential structures may seek to purchase the entire leased site if protection is extended to non-residential buildings before the claim is resolved.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant who is entitled to purchase the leased site must pay the site value fixed by the appellate court where the lower trial-court valuation is not accepted.
material_facts: The trial court fixed a lower value for the site, and the appellate court assessed a higher value.
The tenant asked that the trial court’s lower valuation be restored.
The Supreme Court found no merit in that request and retained the appellate court’s valuation, directing payment by instalments.
issues.conclusion: The appellate court’s valuation stood, and the tenant was required to pay that value on the court-ordered instalment schedule.
issues.legal_principle: The Court upheld the appellate court’s valuation rather than restoring the trial court’s lower figure; it directed payment in instalments. The judgment does not identify a separate statutory provision or earlier case as the basis for this valuation ruling.

predicates.tenant_purchase_entitlement_upheld: The court upheld the tenant’s entitlement to purchase the leased site.
predicates.appellate_court_fixed_site_value_higher_: The appellate court assessed the site at a higher value than the trial court had assessed it.
predicates.tenant_sought_lower_trial_court_value: The tenant asked the court to restore the trial court’s lower valuation.

issues.definition: When purchase entitlement is upheld, the appellate court has fixed a higher site value, and the tenant seeks the lower trial-court value, the tenant must pay the appellate-assessed value on the ordered schedule.
